procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of conviction and sentence (including death sentences and life imprisonment) passed by the Sessions Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Five murder references (due to death sentences) and fourteen appeals by the convicts were filed before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. The High Court confirmed the death sentences and dismissed the appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (convicts) approached the Supreme Court by way of Special Leave Petitions after losing their appeals and having their death sentences confirmed by the High Court.

decision.appeal_result: Appeals Nos. 79/81 & 86 of 1981 are allowed. The rest of the appeals are dismissed.
decision.conviction_status: Set aside for the appellant in Appeals Nos. 79/81 & 86/81. Confirmed for the appellants in the other appeals.
decision.sentence_status: Set aside for the appellant in Appeals Nos. 79/81 & 86/81. Confirmed for the appellants in the other appeals. The sentences of imprisonment for the latter will run concurrently.
directions: The appellant in Appeals Nos. 79/81 & 86/81 (Mohinder Singh) shall be set at liberty forthwith unless he is required to be detained in connection with some other offence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the Sessions Court and the High Court.

facts: The Sessions Court convicted the appellants for various offenses, and the High Court confirmed these convictions.
This created a situation of 'concurrent findings of fact' by two lower courts.
The evidence relied upon by the lower courts included witness testimony and a dying declaration.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence that had been accepted by both the Sessions Court and the High Court.
Regarding witness testimony, the Court noted that the lower courts had accepted it and stated, "We see no reason to do otherwise."
Regarding a dying declaration, the Court observed that both lower courts had found it to be "genuine and true," and stated, "We are of the same opinion."
The Court explicitly stated it saw "no reason to dislodge this concurrent finding of fact" and that it "does not, therefore, call for interfernce at the hands of this Court."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact because it agreed with the assessment of the evidence by the Sessions Court and the High Court and found no reason to overturn their conclusions.

reasoning.conclusion: The Court decided that the death sentence should only be imposed if the circumstances of the crime are such that there is no other alternative. This is a necessary condition, but it is part of a larger test. The court must take a comprehensive view of all circumstances, including mitigating factors for the offender, and find that life imprisonment is a completely inadequate punishment. Therefore, the death penalty is only an option when there is no alternative, establishing it as an exception for the "rarest-of-rare-cases."

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the Sessions Court and the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The evidence provided by the two eyewitnesses, P.W. Amar Singh and P.W. Mohindo, was not reliable enough to be implicitly trusted.
The remaining evidence was neither sufficient nor satisfactory to establish the guilt of the appellant, Machhi Singh.
respondent_arguments: The eyewitnesses were credible and had no reason to concoct a story, as testifying put them at considerable risk.
The evidence of the witnesses was rightly accepted by both the Sessions Court and the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Are the circumstances of the crime such that there is no other alternative but to impose the death sentence?
appellant_arguments: The death sentence imposed on the appellants is not justified.
respondent_arguments: The death sentence imposed by the lower courts should be confirmed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The extreme penalty of death should only be inflicted in the gravest cases of extreme culpability. Life imprisonment is the rule and the death sentence is an exception, to be imposed only when life imprisonment is an altogether inadequate punishment, considering the circumstances of both the crime and the offender.
obiter: Every member of the community owes a debt to the community for its protection. When a killer shows ingratitude, the community may withdraw that protection by sanctioning the death penalty in the rarest of rare cases when its collective conscience is so shocked that it expects the judiciary to inflict the death penalty.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court will not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact from the lower courts regarding the credibility of eyewitnesses, as there was no reason to doubt their testimony and they were unlikely to falsely implicate the appellants at great personal risk. In determining the sentence, the death penalty is to be imposed only in the gravest cases of extreme culpability when life imprisonment is an altogether inadequate punishment, a standard which the community endorses when crimes are particularly abhorrent in their motive or manner of commission.
legal_tests_applied: The extreme penalty of death need not be inflicted except in gravest cases of extreme culpability.

Death sentence must be imposed only when life imprisonment appears to be an altogether inadequate punishment having regard to the relevant circumstances of the crime, and provided, and only provided the option to impose sentence of imprisonment for life cannot be conscientiously exercised having regard to the nature and circumstances of the crime and all the relevant circumstances.

If upon taking an overall global view of all the circumstances in the light of the aforesaid proposition and taking into account the answers to the questions posed herein above, the circumstances of the case are such that death sentence is warranted, the court would proceed to do so.
why_appellant_lost: The Court refused to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact from the Sessions Court and High Court, stating it saw no reason to do otherwise.
The argument that eyewitnesses were unreliable was rejected because the court found it improbable that the witnesses would concoct a story, as testifying exposed them to considerable risk.

For the appellants whose death sentences were confirmed, the circumstances of their crimes were considered grave enough to warrant the extreme penalty, rendering life imprisonment an inadequate punishment.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the eyewitness evidence was credible and rightly accepted by the lower courts was affirmed, with the Court noting the witnesses' presence was natural and their testimony was corroborated.

The Court agreed with the respondent that the death sentence was appropriate for most of the appellants, confirming that the findings of guilt and the sentences imposed by the lower courts should be unhesitatingly confirmed for those cases.
policy_considerations: The Court reasoned that the community as a whole does not endorse a 'death sentence-in-no-case' doctrine because when a person violates the foundational principle of 'reverence for life' by killing another, society may not feel bound by a purely humanistic approach.
Community sentiment in favor of retaining the death penalty is often based on the motive for the crime, the manner of its commission, or its anti-social and abhorrent nature.
